DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekly Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

The study proposes district-wide weekly food waste collection from April 2027. The case rests on three claims:
- a 4,000-household pilot showed strong participation across houses and flats;
- projected tonnage of about 3,290 t a year at Brookfield saves £243,000 in disposal costs;
- a net cost of about £490,000 is covered by a £520,000 provisional allocation.

**The cost arithmetic checks out:**

| Item | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Vehicles | 6 × £165k ÷ 7 years | £141,400 |
| Crews | 12 operatives × £34k | £408,000 |
| Total cost | | £733,400 |
| Net cost | £733,400 − £243,000 | £490,400 |

The pilot rates also follow from the counts (66%, 21% and 57%). The pilot itself is a real strength: it was local, broken down by housing type, measured weekly, and checked for contamination.

Three of the study's central claims don't hold on its own figures, however. Once they are corrected, the service is not fully funded.

## 1. Participation in flats is a third of the rate in houses

Table 1 shows **66% in houses and 21% in flats**. The text calls this "broadly similar" and draws the conclusion of a uniform roll-out from it. The pilot shows the opposite: flats need a different approach, and the study should cost one. Common options are communal bins, bin-store caddies, or extra engagement.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce

§3 applies **64%** participation district-wide. The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and no 64% appears anywhere in it. Applying the pilot's own rates by housing type to the district's 20% share of flats gives:
- houses: 41,600 × 66% × 1.9 kg = about 52,200 kg a week;
- flats: 10,400 × 21% × 1.4 kg = about 3,100 kg a week;
- **total: about 2,870 t a year, not 3,290 t.**

Even this may be optimistic:
- Pilot households received free liners for six months. The roll-out offers only three months' supply, and participation often falls when liners run out.
- The pilot covered only January to June, and a new service often attracts more effort at first than it does later.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

§4 states that Brookfield's contracted capacity is **1,800 t a year until 2029**. Both the study's figure (3,290 t) and the corrected figure (about 2,870 t) exceed this. The saving of £243,000 assumes that every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38, which the study itself shows isn't possible.

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,000 | Covered |
| Corrected tonnage, all at Brookfield | about £212,000 | about £521,000 | **About £1k short** |
| Corrected tonnage, 1,800 t at Brookfield, the remainder saving nothing | about £133,000 | about £600,000 | **About £80k short** |

The surplus of roughly 1,000 t would have to go to the plant 46 miles away. Its gate fee isn't given, and the extra vehicle time and fuel aren't costed. "Treatment is local" is true only for the first 1,800 t.

Ask Brookfield for more capacity, and get a quote, including haulage, from the second plant.

## 4. Costs that may be missing

- **Crew on-costs:** is £34,000 salary alone, or does it include employer NI and pension (often +25–30%)? Cover for leave and sickness also needs extra staff beyond the 12.
- **Not costed:**
  - supervision and route planning;
  - recruitment and training;
  - the dedicated phone line and web page;
  - any depot changes.
- **Upfront cash:**
  - about £990k for vehicles, which must be ordered in December;
  - caddies for 52,000 households.

  The table shows these only as annual depreciation. The study should say how they will be financed and what the financing costs.
- **Incineration contract:** if the residual-waste contract has a minimum-tonnage clause, diverting food waste may not save the full £112 a tonne.

## 5. Funding and timing risk

- **The funding is provisional.** The £520,000 is "provisional" and the government has only "indicated" it will be paid. Even on the study's own figures the margin is £30,000, about 6%. Ordering £990k of vehicles in December before the allocation is confirmed is a risk Cabinet should be told about explicitly.
- **The timetable is tight in March 2027:**
  - vehicles delivered;
  - crews trained on them;
  - caddies sent to all 52,000 households.

  Any slip in vehicle delivery moves the start date.
- **Statutory deadline:** check that April 2027 complies with the law. My understanding is that the general deadline for English councils was 31 March 2026, unless a transitional arrangement applies. If Thornbury relies on one, the study should say so.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Weighted average:** the overall figure of 1.9 kg per participating household is really about 1.86 kg.
- **Satisfaction survey:** "81% of surveyed households" needs a response rate. Satisfied participants are more likely to reply.
- **Vehicle numbers:** if tonnage is lower, it's worth checking whether six vehicles and crews are still needed. Rounds are usually driven by the number of households rather than by weight, so the saving may be small.

## Before Cabinet decides

1. Use the pilot's actual rates by housing type in the projection (about 2,870 t), and explain or remove the 64%.
2. Set out a separate approach for flats, with its cost.
3. Show how tonnage above 1,800 t will be treated, at what cost, and the revised net cost.
4. Confirm crew on-costs and add the missing cost lines.
5. Confirm the funding allocation, or set out what happens if it falls short, before committing to the vehicle order.

**Overall:** the pilot is good evidence, and a roll-out is clearly needed. But the study's own data contradict its three headline claims:
- flats behave very differently from houses;
- the projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce;
- Brookfield can't take the tonnage.

On corrected figures the service costs roughly £520,000–£600,000 a year. Whether the provisional allocation covers that is open, not settled.
